html:
A gold coin first struck by Constantine the Great around 309, at 72 to the Roman pound, about 4.5 grams of nearly pure gold.

It replaced the aureus, which had shrunk during the crises of the third century, when the silver denarius became almost worthless. Constantine paid soldiers and officials in solidi and took taxes in gold, which kept the coin in demand.

The Byzantine Empire kept its weight and purity for some 700 years, until debasement in the 1000s led to its replacement by the hyperpyron in 1092. Called the nomisma in Greek and the bezant in the West, it was trusted from Britain to India, and solidi have turned up in tombs in China. The gold dinar of the caliph Abd al-Malik was modelled on it. Its name lives on in the word soldier, once a man paid in solidi, and in the "s" for shillings in old British money.
sum: A gold coin first struck by Constantine the Great around 309, at 72 to the Roman pound, about 4.5 grams of nearly pure gold.
